questions.a: Yes. We talk first, you fill in a short health questionnaire, and I check how you move before any training. If the questionnaire asks for your GP's go-ahead, we wait for it.

questions.q: I haven't trained for years. Is that all right?
questions.a: Most people I train start that way. The first sessions are lighter than you'd expect.
Session by session, after each one, by bank transfer or card. There is no contract.

questions.q: What if I need to cancel?
questions.a: Cancel 24 hours ahead and there's no charge. Later than that, the session counts.

questions.q: Do you come to my home?
questions.a: Yes, in SW1X, SW3, SW7, SW10 and W8. I bring the equipment; a space the size of a mat is enough.

questions.q: How soon will I see a difference?
questions.a: It depends on you, your week and how often we train. I won't promise a number; we'll agree what to look for and check it every four weeks.
Pay-by-phone bays on the King's Road and the streets around it. The yard itself has no parking.

programmes.title: Programmes
programmes.intro: Four ways I train people. Each only where I hold the qualification for it.

items.name: Strength
items.line: Lifting well, at any age, from the first session.
items.who: Anyone who wants to be stronger, whether you've lifted before or not.
text: We start with how you move, then add weight slowly: squats, hinges, presses and carries, each taught until it's yours.
Every session is written down, so you can see what you lifted last time and what we're aiming at today.

photo.alt: A trainer guiding a woman through a rowing stroke in a bright studio

items.name: Pregnancy and after
items.line: Training through pregnancy and back from it, at your pace.
items.who: Expectant and new mothers, from the first trimester to a year after the birth.
text: Sessions change as you do: what we can keep, what we leave for later, and what helps the weeks after the birth.
After the birth we start once your GP or midwife says so, usually after the six-week check, with breathing and the deep core first.
items.care: Before we start, and again after the birth, I ask for your GP's or midwife's go-ahead. Tell me how you're feeling at every session.
items.qualification: Level 3 Award: Training Pre and Postnatal Clients

photo.alt: A pregnant woman sitting cross-legged on a mat in a pale room

items.name: Back to training
items.line: For a sore back, or after an injury, alongside your physio.
items.who: People with low back pain, or coming back to exercise once a physio or GP has signed them off.
text: We work on what you can do, not on what hurts: walking, then strength, built up a little at a time.
If your physio has given you exercises, bring them. I'll fit our sessions around their plan, not the other way round.
sessions: Strength for the back and hips
items.care: I work alongside your physio or GP. If something new comes up, I'll ask you to see them before we carry on.
items.qualification: Level 4 Certificate in Physical Activity and Lifestyle Strategies for Managing Low Back Pain

text: Forty-five minutes of strength and conditioning, at the start or end of your working day.

stories.intro: Clients on what training here is like.

items.name: Claire
words: I'd never touched a barbell. The first month was mostly learning to stand properly, and I'm glad it was.
Now I look forward to Tuesday mornings, which I never thought I'd say about exercise.

items.name: Tom
words: My physio and Sam spoke before we started. That's what made me trust it.
We went slower than I wanted. He was right.

items.name: Priya
words: I trained until thirty-six weeks and started again at ten weeks after. Every session was different, because I was.

journal.title: Journal
journal.intro: Short pieces on training, written between sessions.

articles.title: Your first barbell
articles.intro: Why we start with an empty bar, and stay there longer than you'd like.

photo.alt: The studio's racks and benches under soft lights

body: Most people's first barbell session is shorter than they expect. We spend it on how you stand, where the bar sits and how you breathe.
The empty bar weighs twenty kilos. That's enough to learn on, and enough to get it wrong if we rush.
Weight goes on once the movement looks the same every time. For some people that's the second week; for others, the fourth. Either is fine.

articles.title: Training in a busy week
articles.intro: Two sessions you'll keep beat four you won't.

photo.alt: A laptop, a mat and a resistance band on a wooden floor

body: When the diary fills up, training is usually the first thing to go. So we plan for the week you'll actually have.
Two fixed hours, early or late, booked like meetings. Then something short for the days between: ten minutes, no kit.

articles.title: What rest days are for
articles.intro: The training happens in the session; the getting stronger happens after.

photo.alt: Two women resting on a sunlit floor after stretching

body: A rest day isn't a day off from the plan. It's part of it.
Walk, sleep, eat well. If you're sore, move gently; if you're tired for days, tell me and we'll change the week.
